info.text:
Giving money or investments this Christmas? Canada has no gift tax, and a gift you receive isn't income. But some gifts can still cost the person who gives them.

1) Money you give your spouse or common-law partner to invest: the interest, dividends and capital gains are taxed to you (the attribution rules). Exception: money your spouse puts into their own TFSA isn't attributed back to you.

2) Money you give kids under 18 (children, grandchildren, other related minors): interest and dividends are taxed to you.

3) Gifts that aren't cash (shares, a cottage, crypto) to anyone but your spouse: CRA treats it as sold at fair market value.
Example: shares bought for $10,000 and worth $30,000, given to your adult son → you report a $20,000 capital gain; half of it, $10,000, is added to your income. His cost becomes $30,000.

4) Gifts from your employer: non-cash gifts and awards up to $500 a year in total are tax-free (only the excess is taxable). Cash and near-cash gifts are always taxable.

The gift itself is tax-free. What it earns, and what grew before you gave it, may not be. Exceptions exist (prescribed-rate loans, principal residence, separation); ask a professional before a large gift.

Next: down on a stock? Why December 30 matters.

Sources: CRA, Amounts that are not reported or taxed; Transfers of capital property; T4037; How to contribute to a TFSA; Gifts, awards and long-service awards (canada.ca). The family and the shares are an example. General information, not advice.

info.text:
Down on a stock this year? In Canada, a capital loss can offset your capital gains, but only if the sale lands in the right year.

The rule: capital losses offset capital gains only (not your salary or other income).
Example: a $12,000 gain on one stock and an $8,000 loss on another. Sell the loser and your net gain is $4,000; half is taxable, so $2,000 instead of $6,000.

Why December 30 (2026): Canadian trades settle one business day later (T+1), and CRA treats the settlement date as the date you sold. A trade on Wednesday, December 30 settles December 31; a December 31 trade settles in 2027. Confirm the cut-off with your broker.

The trap: if you or an affiliated person (like your spouse) buys the same stock within 30 days before or after the sale and still holds it 30 days later, it's a superficial loss and the loss is denied. It usually gets added to the cost of the shares bought back instead.

Losses inside a TFSA or RRSP can't be claimed at all.

Next: investments outside Canada, and the CRA form you can't skip.

Sources: CRA, Capital losses; What is a superficial loss; T4037 (canada.ca); CRA interpretation 2012-0468931C6 (settlement date); Canadian Securities Administrators (T+1, 2024). The numbers are an example. General information, not advice.
